memory_text: During Dashain, smoke rose from every kitchen as relatives returned along the hill paths to the ancestral house. Elders pressed red tika and fresh jamara onto each forehead, speaking blessings for courage and a long life. Children crossed the whole village collecting blessings, but the true celebration was seeing an empty courtyard become a family again.

At Tihar we made a trail of oil lamps from the courtyard to the prayer room to welcome Laxmi. After dusk, groups moved from door to door singing deusi and bhailo; no doorway stayed dark or silent. Sisters wove marigold garlands for Bhai Tika, and neighbours sent plates of sel roti between homes.

Gundruk began after the mustard and radish harvest. We wilted the leaves in the sun, crushed them until their scent changed, packed them tightly into an earthen pot, and sealed it warm beside the hearth. When the sourness was right, the whole family spread the leaves on a clean mat to dry—summer greens saved for a winter bowl of soup.

The terraces were repaired before the monsoon, each stone wall holding both soil and the labour of earlier generations. We guided water from the upper field to the lower one with small mud gates, never taking more than our turn. Households exchanged rice seedlings so one failed nursery would not ruin a family’s year.

Our village spring was said to have appeared where a tired traveller struck the earth with a walking stick. At dawn, people waited with brass vessels and exchanged the day’s first news beside the water. Nobody washed clothes at the source; the old story carried a practical promise to keep everyone’s drinking water clean.

We say ‘thuchi che’ to offer thanks. Children learned to say it to people and quietly after receiving food or shelter. The words were small, but elders treated them as a daily practice: gratitude should be spoken before abundance is taken for granted.

Before every child could afford paper, we spread fine dust across a wooden board and traced letters with a fingertip, smoothing the surface to begin again. Older pupils led multiplication tables beneath the pipal tree. If one voice faltered, the others carried it until the lesson belonged to everyone.

A bamboo doko is woven from the base upward, with every crossing tightened against the last. My father let my hands make loose, crooked patterns and then undid them beside me without anger. He said a strong basket comes only after learning that beginning again is part of the craft.
